### Evidence Notes

#### Problem and Prior Work
Recurrent neural networks compute hidden states $h_t$ sequentially as a function of previous states $h_{t-1}$ and input position $t$, preventing parallelization within training sequences and constraining batching at longer sequence lengths [p00007]. While convolutional alternatives (such as Extended Neural GPU, ByteNet, and ConvS2S) compute representations in parallel, the number of operations required to connect signals between distant positions grows linearly (ConvS2S) or logarithmically (ByteNet) with distance [p00010].

#### Mechanisms and Design Rationales
The Transformer is an auto-regressive encoder-decoder architecture that eliminates recurrence and convolutions, relying entirely on self-attention [p00002, p00013, p00015]. Relating any two positions takes a constant number of operations, though the authors note this risks reduced effective resolution from averaging attention weights, which they address via multi-head attention [p00010].

The encoder comprises a stack of $N=6$ identical layers, each containing two sub-layers: multi-head self-attention and a position-wise fully connected feed-forward network [p00017]. The decoder comprises a stack of $N=6$ identical layers containing three sub-layers: masked multi-head self-attention, multi-head cross-attention over the encoder output stack, and a position-wise feed-forward network [p00018]. Every sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalization, computing $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$, maintaining a uniform output dimension of $d_{\text{model}} = 512$ across all sub-layers and embedding layers [p00017, p00018]. Decoder self-attention is masked and target embeddings are offset by one position to prevent positions from attending to subsequent tokens [p00018].

Attention maps a query matrix $Q$, key matrix $K$ (both dimension $d_k$), and value matrix $V$ (dimension $d_v$) to outputs via scaled dot-product attention:
$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$
[p00020, p00022]. The scaling factor $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ is introduced because the authors suspect that for large $d_k$, large dot-product magnitudes push softmax into regions with vanishingly small gradients [p00024].

#### Exact Results and Settings
On WMT 2014 English-to-German translation, the model achieves 28.4 BLEU, exceeding existing results including ensembles by over 2 BLEU [p00002]. On WMT 2014 English-to-French, it reaches a single-model state of the art of 41.8 BLEU after 3.5 days of training on eight GPUs [p00002]. A translation state of the art can be reached in 12 hours on eight P100 GPUs [p00009]. The architecture also applies to English constituency parsing [p00002].

#### Assumptions and Limitations
Decoder generation is inherently auto-regressive and consumes previously generated symbols one element at a time during decoding [p00015]. The hypothesis regarding vanishing gradients at large $d_k$ is stated as an author suspicion rather than a proven theorem [p00024].

sources.text: Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states $h_t$ , as a function of the previous hidden state $h_{t-1}$ and the input for position $t$ . This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples. Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter. The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains.

The goal of reducing sequential computation also forms the foundation of the Extended Neural GPU [16], ByteNet [18] and ConvS2S [9], all of which use convolutional neural networks as basic building block, computing hidden representations in parallel for all input and output positions. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes it more difficult to learn dependencies between distant positions [12]. In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2.

The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence-aligned RNNs or convolution. In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention and discuss its advantages over models such as [17]; [18] and [9].

Most competitive neural sequence transduction models have an encoder-decoder structure [5]; [2]; [35]. Here, the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations $(x_1, ..., x_n)$ to a sequence of continuous representations $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_n)$ . Given $\mathbf{z}$ , the decoder then generates an output sequence $(y_1,...,y_m)$ of symbols one element at a time. At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next.

The encoder is composed of a stack of $N=6$ identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. We employ a residual connection [11] around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization [1]. That is, the output of each sub-layer is $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$ , where $\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)$ is the function implemented by the sub-layer itself. To facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension $d_{\text{model}}=512$ .

The decoder is also composed of a stack of $N=6$ identical layers. In addition to the two sub-layers in each encoder layer, the decoder inserts a third sub-layer, which performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack. Similar to the encoder, we employ residual connections around each of the sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. We also modify the self-attention sub-layer in the decoder stack to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions. This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position $i$ can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than $i$ .

We call our particular attention "Scaled Dot-Product Attention" (Figure 2). The input consists of queries and keys of dimension $d_k$ , and values of dimension $d_v$ . We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by $\sqrt{d_k}$ , and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.
$\begin{equation} \mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}})V \end{equation}$

While for small values of $d_k$ the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of $d_k$ [3]. We suspect that for large values of $d_k$ , the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients 1. To counteract this effect, we scale the dot products by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}$ .

In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output. The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.
The Transformer - model architecture.

The Transformer follows this overall architecture using stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers for both the encoder and decoder, shown in the left and right halves of Figure 1, respectively.

### Evidence Notes

#### Mechanisms and Design Rationales
Multi-head attention projects queries, keys, and values $h$ times using learned parameter matrices $W_i^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}$, $W_i^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_k}$, and $W_i^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_v}$ [p00026, p00028, p00029]. Scaled dot-product attention runs concurrently on each projection; the resulting $d_v$-dimensional outputs are concatenated and projected through $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{\text{model}}}$ [p00026, p00028, p00029]. This allows simultaneous attention to information from different representation subspaces at different positions, which single-head averaging inhibits [p00027]. The model sets $h=8$ and $d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}/h = 64$, keeping total computational cost close to single-head attention with full dimensionality [p00030].

Multi-head attention operates in three configurations:
1. Encoder-decoder attention, where queries originate from the preceding decoder layer and keys and values originate from the encoder output [p00032].
2. Encoder self-attention, where queries, keys, and values all derive from the prior encoder layer [p00033].
3. Decoder self-attention, where positions attend only to positions up to and including themselves by setting illegal softmax inputs to $-\infty$ [p00034].

Each layer also includes a position-wise feed-forward network consisting of two linear transformations with an inner ReLU activation: $\mathrm{FFN}(x) = \max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2$ [p00035, p00036]. Parameters differ across layers, with inner dimensionality $d_{ff}=2048$ and input/output dimensionality $d_{\text{model}}=512$ [p00037]. Input and output embedding layers share weights with the pre-softmax linear transformation and are scaled by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$ [p00038]. 

To convey token order, fixed sinusoidal positional encodings of dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ are added to input embeddings [p00039, p00041]. The authors hypothesize this facilitates learning relative attention because offsets represent linear functions of position [p00042].

#### Comparisons and Complexity
Per-layer comparison across layer types for sequence length $n$, dimension $d$, and kernel size $k$ establishes [p00048]:
- Self-attention: $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ complexity, $O(1)$ sequential operations, $O(1)$ maximum path length [p00048].
- Recurrent: $O(n \cdot d^2)$ complexity, $O(n)$ sequential operations, $O(n)$ maximum path length [p00048].
- Convolutional: $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$ complexity, $O(1)$ sequential operations, $O(\log_k(n))$ maximum path length [p00048].
Self-attention is computationally faster than recurrence when $n < d$, typical for word-piece and byte-pair representations [p00049]. Separable convolutions achieve complexity $O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$, equaling self-attention plus a point-wise layer when $k=n$ [p00050].

#### Ablations, Assumptions, and Limitations
Learned positional embeddings yielded nearly identical results to sinusoidal encodings (Table 3, row E); sinusoids were retained for hypothetical extrapolation to longer sequences [p00043]. Self-attention exhibits quadratic complexity $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ with respect to sequence length [p00048]. Restricting self-attention to neighborhood size $r$ reduces complexity to $O(r \cdot n \cdot d)$ but increases maximum path length to $O(n/r)$; this remained untested future work [p00048, p00049].

sources.text: Instead of performing a single attention function with $d_{\text{model}}$ -dimensional keys, values and queries, we found it beneficial to linearly project the queries, keys and values $h$ times with different, learned linear projections to $d_k$ , $d_k$ and $d_v$ dimensions, respectively. On each of these projected versions of queries, keys and values we then perform the attention function in parallel, yielding $d_v$ -dimensional output values. These are concatenated and once again projected, resulting in the final values, as depicted in Figure 2.

$\begin{align*} \mathrm{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) &= \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head_1}, ..., \mathrm{head_h})W^O\\ % \mathrm{where} \mathrm{head_i} &= \mathrm{Attention}(QW_Q_i^{\dmodel \times d_q}, KW_K_i^{\dmodel \times d_k}, VW^V_i^{\dmodel \times d_v})\\ \text{where}~\mathrm{head_i} &= \mathrm{Attention}(QW^Q_i, KW^K_i, VW^V_i)\\ \end{align*}$

Where the projections are parameter matrices $W^Q_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$ , $W^K_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$ , $W^V_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_v}$ and $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{\text{model}}}$ .
Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

In this work we employ $h=8$ parallel attention layers, or heads. For each of these we use $d_k=d_v=d_{\text{model}}/h=64$ . Due to the reduced dimension of each head, the total computational cost is similar to that of single-head attention with full dimensionality.

sources.text: Similarly, self-attention layers in the decoder allow each position in the decoder to attend to all positions in the decoder up to and including that position. We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property. We implement this inside of scaled dot-product attention by masking out (setting to $-\infty$ ) all values in the input of the softmax which correspond to illegal connections. See Figure 2.

In addition to attention sub-layers, each of the layers in our encoder and decoder contains a fully connected feed-forward network, which is applied to each position separately and identically. This consists of two linear transformations with a ReLU activation in between.
$\begin{equation} \mathrm{FFN}(x)=\max(0, xW_1 + b_1) W_2 + b_2 \end{equation}$

While the linear transformations are the same across different positions, they use different parameters from layer to layer. Another way of describing this is as two convolutions with kernel size 1. The dimensionality of input and output is $d_{\text{model}}=512$ , and the inner-layer has dimensionality $d_{ff}=2048$ .

Similarly to other sequence transduction models, we use learned embeddings to convert the input tokens and output tokens to vectors of dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ . We also use the usual learned linear transformation and softmax function to convert the decoder output to predicted next-token probabilities. In our model, we share the same weight matrix between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation, similar to [30]. In the embedding layers, we multiply those weights by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$ .

Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence. To this end, we add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks. The positional encodings have the same dimension $d_{\text{model}}$ as the embeddings, so that the two can be summed. There are many choices of positional encodings, learned and fixed [9].
$\begin{align*} PE_{(pos,2i)} = sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}) \\ PE_{(pos,2i+1)} = cos(pos / 10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}) \end{align*}$

where $pos$ is the position and $i$ is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from $2\pi$ to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$ . We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset $k$ , $PE_{pos+k}$ can be represented as a linear function of $PE_{pos}$ .

Layer Type Complexity per Layer Sequential Maximum Path Length Operations Self-Attention $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ $O(1)$ $O(1)$ Recurrent $O(n \cdot d^2)$ $O(n)$ $O(n)$ Convolutional $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$ $O(1)$ $O(log_k(n))$ Self-Attention (restricted) $O(r \cdot n \cdot d)$ $O(1)$ $O(n/r)$

As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires $O(n)$ sequential operations. In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length $n$ is smaller than the representation dimensionality $d$ , which is most often the case with sentence representations used by state-of-the-art models in machine translations, such as word-piece [38] and byte-pair [31] representations. To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size $r$ in the input sequence centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to $O(n/r)$ . We plan to investigate this approach further in future work.

A single convolutional layer with kernel width $k < n$ does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Doing so requires a stack of $O(n/k)$ convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels, or $O(log_k(n))$ in the case of dilated convolutions [18], increasing the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network. Convolutional layers are generally more expensive than recurrent layers, by a factor of $k$ . Separable convolutions [6], however, decrease the complexity considerably, to $O(k \cdot n \cdot d + n \cdot d^2)$ . Even with $k=n$ , however, the complexity of a separable convolution is equal to the combination of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed-forward layer, the approach we take in our model.

We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E)). We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.

### Evidence Notes

#### Training Settings and Optimization
- **Data & Batching**: WMT 2014 English-German (EN-DE) contains approximately 4.5 million sentence pairs encoded with byte-pair encoding into a shared source-target vocabulary of about 37,000 tokens [p00053]. WMT 2014 English-French (EN-FR) contains 36 million sentences split into a 32,000 word-piece vocabulary [p00053]. Batches are grouped by approximate sequence length, containing roughly 25,000 source and 25,000 target tokens [p00053].
- **Hardware & Schedule**: Training used one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs [p00054]. The base model ran for 100,000 steps (0.4 s/step, total 12 hours) [p00054]. The big model ran for 300,000 steps (1.0 s/step, total 3.5 days) [p00054].
- **Optimizer**: Adam optimizer with $\beta_1=0.9$, $\beta_2=0.98$, $\epsilon=10^{-9}$ [p00055]. Learning rate varied per:
  $$\text{lrate} = d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5} \cdot \min(\text{step\_num}^{-0.5}, \text{step\_num} \cdot \text{warmup\_steps}^{-1.5})$$
  linearly increasing for $\text{warmup\_steps}=4000$, then decaying proportionally to $\text{step\_num}^{-0.5}$ [p00056, p00057].
- **Regularization**: 
  - Residual dropout ($P_{drop}=0.1$ for base model) is applied to sub-layer outputs before addition and normalization, and to the sums of embeddings and positional encodings [p00059]. Big model EN-FR used $P_{drop}=0.1$, whereas big EN-DE used $0.3$ [p00063, p00066].
  - Label smoothing $\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$ was applied; authors note it hurts perplexity because the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU [p00060].
- **Inference**: Beam search with beam size 4, length penalty $\alpha=0.6$, and maximum output length of input length + 50 [p00064]. For base models, the last 5 checkpoints (written at 10-minute intervals) were averaged; for big models, the last 20 checkpoints were averaged [p00064].

#### Exact Results: Machine Translation
- **WMT 2014 English-to-German**: Transformer (base) achieved 27.3 BLEU ($3.3 \cdot 10^{18}$ FLOPs); Transformer (big) achieved 28.4 BLEU ($2.3 \cdot 10^{19}$ FLOPs), surpassing previous models and ensembles by over 2.0 BLEU [p00061, p00062].
- **WMT 2014 English-to-French**: Transformer (base) achieved 38.1 BLEU; Transformer (big) reached 41.8 BLEU in Table 2 summary text (reported as 41.0 BLEU in paragraph text [p00063]) at $2.3 \cdot 10^{19}$ FLOPs, outperforming prior single models [p00061, p00063].

#### Exact Results: English Constituency Parsing
- Challenges: Strongly constrained output, longer than input, and RNN sequence-to-sequence models previously struggled in small-data regimes [p00071].
- Architecture & Settings: 4-layer Transformer, $d_{\text{model}}=1024$, beam size 21, $\alpha=0.3$, max output length input + 300 [p00072, p00073].
- WSJ Section 23 F1:
  - WSJ-only discriminative (40K sentences, 16K vocabulary): 91.3 F1, outperforming BerkeleyParser (90.4) and Vinyals & Kaiser (88.3), trailing Dyer et al. (91.7) [p00070, p00072, p00075].
  - Semi-supervised (17M sentences, 32K vocabulary): 92.7 F1, outperforming Vinyals & Kaiser (92.1) and McClosky et al. (92.1), trailing generative Dyer et al. (93.3) and multi-task Luong et al. (93.0) [p00070, p00072].

#### Model Variations and Ablations (Table 3, newstest2013 dev set)
Evaluated without checkpoint averaging [p00067]:
- **Attention heads ($h$)**: Single-head attention ($h=1, d_k=d_v=512$) dropped BLEU to 24.9 (0.9 BLEU worse than base 25.8 with $h=8$); too many heads ($h=32, d_k=16$) also degraded BLEU (25.4) [p00066, p00068].
- **Key size ($d_k$)**: Reducing key dimension hurt quality ($d_k=16 \to 25.1$ BLEU; $d_k=32 \to 25.4$ BLEU), leading authors to suggest compatibility is difficult and dot product may benefit from more sophisticated functions [p00066, p00069].
- **Size and dropout**: Larger models improved performance ($d_{\text{model}}=1024 \to 26.0$ BLEU; big model with 213M parameters $\to 26.4$ BLEU); dropout was essential to avoid overfitting ($P_{drop}=0.0 \to 24.6$ BLEU) [p00066, p00069].
- **Positional embedding**: Learned positional embeddings yielded 25.7 BLEU, nearly identical to sinusoidal base (25.8 BLEU) [p00066, p00069].

Sentence pairs were batched together by approximate sequence length. Each training batch contained a set of sentence pairs containing approximately 25000 source tokens and 25000 target tokens.

### Evidence Notes

#### Conclusions and Stated Future Work
The Transformer is presented as the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention, eliminating recurrence in encoder-decoder architectures in favor of multi-headed self-attention [p00077]. For translation, the model trains faster than recurrent or convolutional models while establishing a new state of the art on WMT 2014 English-to-German and English-to-French benchmarks [p00078]. Authors plan future extensions to non-text modalities (images, audio, video), research into local restricted attention mechanisms to process large inputs/outputs efficiently, and non-sequential generation methods [p00079]. Training and evaluation code is publicly released [p00080].

#### Qualitative Self-Attention Behaviors
Visualizations of encoder self-attention at layer 5 (of 6 layers) indicate that individual attention heads learn distinct behaviors without explicit syntactic supervision [p00122, p00123, p00124]:
- **Long-distance dependencies**: Multiple heads resolve long-range relationships, such as connecting the verb "making" across an intervening phrase to "more" and "difficult" to complete the construction "making...more difficult" [p00122].
- **Anaphora resolution**: Specific heads track coreference, connecting the possessive pronoun "its" sharply to its antecedent noun phrase "Law" and following noun "application" [p00123].
- **Syntactic and structural relations**: Distinct heads track sentence structure across various token spans, demonstrating specialized roles across parallel heads within the same layer [p00124].

For translation tasks, the Transformer can be trained significantly faster than architectures based on recurrent or convolutional layers. We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video. Making generation less sequential is another research goals of ours.

The Transformer architecture provides an auto-regressive sequence transduction framework that eliminates recurrence and convolutions entirely, relying instead on multi-head self-attention and point-wise feed-forward networks [p00002, p00013, p00015]. 

The primary structural mechanisms are detailed across three framework diagrams:
- **Figure 1** outlines the complete encoder-decoder topology [p00014]. An explanation cannot simplify away its separate $N\times$ stacked layers, the residual skip connections wrapping every sub-layer followed by layer normalization, the three functional attention types, and the dual routing of the encoder stack's output into the decoder cross-attention sub-layers [p00014, p00017, p00018].
- **Figure 2 (left)** defines scaled dot-product attention [p00025]. It specifies the sequential execution: multiplying query matrix $Q$ with key matrix $K$, scaling by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$, applying optional masking, normalizing via softmax, and multiplying by value matrix $V$ [p00020, p00022, p00025].
- **Figure 2 (right)** details multi-head attention [p00025]. Queries, keys, and values are independently projected $h$ times across distinct learned matrices, evaluated in parallel by scaled dot-product attention, concatenated, and projected through an output parameter matrix [p00026, p00028, p00029].

Multi-head attention supports the central contribution by connecting any two sequence positions in $O(1)$ operations and sequential steps, contrasting with $O(n)$ steps in recurrent networks and $O(\log_k n)$ path lengths in convolutional architectures [p00010, p00048]. Projecting across $h=8$ parallel subspaces overcomes the resolution loss of averaging attention weights [p00010, p00027, p00030]. Qualitative visual evidence demonstrates that individual attention heads specialize without explicit syntactic supervision, simultaneously resolving long-distance dependencies (e.g., "making...more difficult") [p00122], anaphoric coreference (e.g., resolving "its" to "Law" and "application") [p00123], and local structural relationships [p00124].

In machine translation, the model establishes state-of-the-art results:
- **WMT 2014 English-to-German**: Transformer (big) reaches 28.4 BLEU, exceeding existing models and ensembles by over 2.0 BLEU [p00002, p00062].
- **WMT 2014 English-to-French**: Table 2 summary text reports 41.8 BLEU for the big model (contrasting with 41.0 BLEU reported in the paragraph text) [p00002, p00061, p00063], achieved after 3.5 days of training on eight P100 GPUs [p00054, p00063]. The base model attains 27.3 BLEU on English-to-German in 12 hours [p00054, p00062].
- **English Constituency Parsing**: In a discriminative WSJ-only setting (40K sentences), a 4-layer model achieves 91.3 F1, outperforming baseline sequence-to-sequence models (88.3) while trailing Dyer et al. (91.7) [p00070, p00072, p00075].

Documented limitations include $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ computational complexity per layer with sequence length $n$, auto-regressive generation that remains strictly sequential during inference, and unproven hypotheses regarding softmax gradient vanishing at large $d_k$ [p00015, p00024, p00048]. Restricting self-attention to local neighborhoods of size $r$ to mitigate quadratic scaling was proposed but left as untested future work [p00048, p00049].

sources.text: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence-aligned RNNs or convolution. In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention and discuss its advantages over models such as [17]; [18] and [9].

Most competitive neural sequence transduction models have an encoder-decoder structure [5]; [2]; [35]. Here, the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations $(x_1, ..., x_n)$ to a sequence of continuous representations $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, ..., z_n)$ . Given $\mathbf{z}$ , the decoder then generates an output sequence $(y_1,...,y_m)$ of symbols one element at a time. At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next.
The Transformer - model architecture.

The encoder is composed of a stack of $N=6$ identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, position-wise fully connected feed-forward network. We employ a residual connection [11] around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization [1]. That is, the output of each sub-layer is $\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x))$ , where $\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)$ is the function implemented by the sub-layer itself. To facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension $d_{\text{model}}=512$ .

The decoder is also composed of a stack of $N=6$ identical layers. In addition to the two sub-layers in each encoder layer, the decoder inserts a third sub-layer, which performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack. Similar to the encoder, we employ residual connections around each of the sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. We also modify the self-attention sub-layer in the decoder stack to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions. This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position $i$ can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than $i$ .
Scaled Dot-Product Attention Multi-Head Attention (left) Scaled Dot-Product Attention. (right) Multi-Head Attention consists of several attention layers running in parallel.

We call our particular attention "Scaled Dot-Product Attention" (Figure 2). The input consists of queries and keys of dimension $d_k$ , and values of dimension $d_v$ . We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by $\sqrt{d_k}$ , and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.
$\begin{equation} \mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}})V \end{equation}$

Instead of performing a single attention function with $d_{\text{model}}$ -dimensional keys, values and queries, we found it beneficial to linearly project the queries, keys and values $h$ times with different, learned linear projections to $d_k$ , $d_k$ and $d_v$ dimensions, respectively. On each of these projected versions of queries, keys and values we then perform the attention function in parallel, yielding $d_v$ -dimensional output values. These are concatenated and once again projected, resulting in the final values, as depicted in Figure 2.

$\begin{align*} \mathrm{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) &= \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head_1}, ..., \mathrm{head_h})W^O\\ % \mathrm{where} \mathrm{head_i} &= \mathrm{Attention}(QW_Q_i^{\dmodel \times d_q}, KW_K_i^{\dmodel \times d_k}, VW^V_i^{\dmodel \times d_v})\\ \text{where}~\mathrm{head_i} &= \mathrm{Attention}(QW^Q_i, KW^K_i, VW^V_i)\\ \end{align*}$

Where the projections are parameter matrices $W^Q_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$ , $W^K_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$ , $W^V_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_v}$ and $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{hd_v \times d_{\text{model}}}$ .

The goal of reducing sequential computation also forms the foundation of the Extended Neural GPU [16], ByteNet [18] and ConvS2S [9], all of which use convolutional neural networks as basic building block, computing hidden representations in parallel for all input and output positions. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes it more difficult to learn dependencies between distant positions [12]. In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2.
